opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it starts with questioning the framing itself. The "arms race" narrative tends to become self-fulfilling. If every major actor believes the others are racing toward some decisive strategic advantage, then the rational-seeming move is to race too, and you get exactly the dynamic everyone says they want to avoid. So part of the work is just not buying into the story that whoever builds the most powerful system first wins everything. I'm skeptical of that story on the merits, and I think it's actively dangerous as a coordinating belief.

Second, I think we underrate how much shared interest there actually is. No government wants systems it can't control, or systems that can be easily misused by non-state actors, or an information ecosystem that collapses into noise. Those are common problems, and common problems are where cooperation has historically been possible, even between rivals. The Cold War gave us arms control agreements, hotlines, and verification regimes, not because the U.S. and the Soviet Union trusted each other, but because they built mechanisms that didn't require trust.

That points to something I care about as a technical researcher: a lot of what makes cooperation hard is a verification problem. Can you credibly show that you're not training a certain kind of system, or that a deployed system has certain properties? There's real research to be done on compute governance, on auditing, on evaluations that different parties can actually agree on. If we can make commitments verifiable, agreements become much more stable.

And then there's a values dimension. A lot of my work is on pluralistic alignment, the idea that AI shouldn't be aligned to one person's or one country's preferences, but should be able to serve people with genuinely different values and norms. If the vision for AI is "my values win," then of course it looks like a zero-sum race. If the vision is AI systems that support fair cooperation among people who disagree, then it's much less threatening for others to participate in building that, and there's more room for a shared project.

So I'd say: resist the race narrative, focus on concrete shared risks, invest in verification so trust isn't required, and articulate a vision of AI that's not about one side dominating. None of that is easy, but I think it's more tractable than people sometimes assume.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention decentralized AI development or distributing its economic benefits broadly.

r002.rationale: It questions the belief that the first builder wins everything, but does not argue that the race offers little incentive if no technology provides a decisive strategic advantage.

r003.rationale: It points to Cold War arms control agreements, hotlines, and verification regimes as models for cooperation between rivals, and applies verification mechanisms to AI.

r004.rationale: The response discusses shared risks and pluralistic alignment, but not sharing AI benefits with countries trailing in development to reduce conflict incentives.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that the framing of an "arms race" is partly a choice, and the way we talk about it shapes whether it actually happens. If the dominant narrative in Washington and Beijing is "whoever gets to AGI first wins everything," then both sides have an incentive to cut corners on safety, and the race becomes self-fulfilling. So part of the work is just resisting that framing, and being honest that it rests on some pretty shaky assumptions, like that there's a single finish line, or that a lead of a few months translates into decisive strategic advantage. I'm not convinced either of those is true.

The second thing is that I don't think avoiding a race means pretending the geopolitical competition doesn't exist. It does. But there's a lot of space between "full cooperation" and "unconstrained race." Historically, even adversaries who deeply distrusted each other managed to agree on things like nuclear test bans, hotlines, verification regimes, because they recognized shared interests in not blowing themselves up. With AI, I think there's a similar set of shared interests. Nobody wants a system that escapes human control, nobody wants AI-enabled bioweapons proliferating to non-state actors, and nobody really wants to be in a world where critical infrastructure is being attacked by autonomous cyber agents. Those are areas where you can imagine concrete agreements, even if they're narrow at first.

The third piece, and this is where my own research interests come in, is the technical side of making agreements enforceable. A lot of what makes arms control hard is verification. How do you know the other side is actually complying? With AI, the compute supply chain is actually unusually concentrated and legible compared to, say, bioweapons. Frontier training runs require huge numbers of specialized chips from a very small number of suppliers. That creates a genuine opportunity for verification mechanisms, things like hardware-enabled governance, where you can attest to what a chip cluster is doing without exposing the model weights or the training data. I think that kind of technical infrastructure for trust is massively underinvested in relative to how important it could be.

And then I'd add a more philosophical point. I think a lot of the race dynamics come from a fairly impoverished picture of what we're racing toward. If you believe the goal is to build a single superintelligent agent that will do everything, then it feels natural that it's winner-take-all. But I actually think that's not the kind of AI we should be building, for safety reasons and for reasons about what's good for people. If instead the goal is something more like AI as infrastructure, systems that help humans coordinate, reason, and act on their values, then the competitive logic looks very different. It's much more like competing over who builds the best internet protocols than who builds the biggest bomb. And competition in that space can actually be healthy.

So I guess my overall view is: push back on the inevitability narrative, find the narrow but real areas of shared interest, invest heavily in verification technology so that agreements can actually hold, and try to shift the goal of the field toward forms of AI where racing isn't the dominant dynamic in the first place. None of that is easy, but I don't think it's hopeless either.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI as infrastructure that can help people, but it does not express hope that decentralized development will distribute AI’s economic benefits more broadly.

r002.rationale: It questions whether a short lead or a single finish line would confer decisive strategic advantage, undermining the winner-take-all incentive behind an arms race.

r003.rationale: It cites nuclear test bans, hotlines, and verification regimes as examples of adversaries agreeing on shared interests, and applies that lesson to AI.

r004.rationale: The response identifies shared safety interests but does not suggest sharing AI benefits with countries trailing in development to reduce their incentive for conflict.

astra-6.text:
I think the first step is to recognize that an arms race isn’t inevitable. It depends on what countries believe about one another’s intentions, and whether they think restraint will be reciprocated. If everyone assumes that everyone else is racing toward systems that could give them a decisive advantage, then racing can start to look like the only reasonable response—even if everyone would prefer a different outcome.

So we need to make mutual restraint credible. That means communication between countries, shared standards for evaluating dangerous capabilities, and verification mechanisms that give each side some confidence that agreements are actually being followed. Expressing good intentions is useful, but it doesn’t resolve the underlying security dilemma.

I also think the way we describe AI matters. If we frame it primarily as a tool for national dominance, we reinforce the incentives we’re trying to escape. There are substantial benefits that countries could pursue together, including scientific research and work on AI safety.

None of that requires assuming that governments will suddenly trust one another. The question is whether we can build arrangements in which cooperation is possible despite distrust, and in which taking a cautious step doesn’t mean accepting an unacceptable disadvantage. That seems like the central challenge to me.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention decentralized AI development or say it would distribute economic benefits more broadly.

r002.rationale: It says fears of a decisive advantage can make racing seem reasonable, but does not argue that an arms race offers little incentive when no technology confers such an advantage.

r003.rationale: The response discusses communication, standards, and verification, but does not identify lessons from maintaining nuclear peace.

r004.rationale: It mentions benefits countries could pursue together, but does not propose sharing benefits with countries trailing in AI or connect that sharing to reduced conflict incentives.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to recognize that an arms race isn’t inevitable. It’s partly a consequence of what people believe about one another. If everyone assumes that the other side will race ahead regardless of the risks, then racing starts to look like the only reasonable response. But collectively, that can leave everyone worse off.

So I would focus on creating conditions where restraint is credible and reciprocal. That means communication between countries, agreements on what kinds of development or deployment are unacceptable, and ways to verify that those agreements are being followed. You want cooperation to be something countries can justify in terms of their own security, rather than something that depends on simply trusting one another.

And I think it helps to distinguish competition over beneficial applications from competition to build increasingly powerful systems without adequate control. There’s room for countries to pursue prosperity and scientific progress while recognizing that some risks are shared. The challenge is to build institutions that make that distinction meaningful in practice.

r001.rationale: The response discusses cooperation and shared risks, but does not express hope that decentralized AI development will spread economic benefits more broadly.

r002.rationale: It says an arms race is not inevitable, but does not argue that no AI technology offers a decisive strategic advantage or that this would reduce incentives to race.

r003.rationale: It recommends communication, agreements, and verification, but does not identify lessons from maintaining nuclear peace.

r004.rationale: It mentions shared risks and beneficial applications, but does not suggest sharing AI benefits with countries trailing in development to reduce conflict incentives.
